findings.title: Permission-denial cache key collides across identity types sharing the same UID
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action, checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)` (defined in pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go) builds the cache key purely from the parsed subject UID, action, name and parent folder, without including the identity type. Anonymous subjects ("anonymous:0") and the render-service subject ("render:0") both resolve to UserUID=="0" (see the test file's own usage of these literal subjects), so a denial recorded for one identity type (e.g. render service denied on some action) will be returned for the other identity type (e.g. an anonymous user) on the next Check call for the same namespace/action/name/folder, even though their actual permission semantics (getRendererPermissions vs getAnonymousPermissions) are completely different and unrelated. Unlike the existing permCache which deliberately uses separate key schemes per identity type (userPermCacheKey vs anonymousPermCacheKey, and no caching at all for render), this new denial cache does not preserve that separation. The result is an incorrect deny being served to a different identity than the one it was computed for, causing availability/correctness regressions (legitimate requests incorrectly denied) that only clear once the 30s denial TTL expires.

findings.title: "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" test doesn't actually exercise the override behavior it claims to test
findings.body: In TestService_CacheCheck's "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" subtest, the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the code sets `s.permCache.Set(ctx, userPermCacheKey(...), map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false})` — i.e. it stores `false`, not `true`. Because the stored value is already `false`, `checkPermission` would return `allowed=false` from this cache entry on its own, and the subsequent default fakeStore (unset in this subtest) also returns no permissions, so the test would still pass (assert resp.Allowed == false) even if the new permDenialCache short-circuit logic were removed entirely. The test therefore does not actually validate that the denial cache takes precedence over a cached "allow" entry, which is the behavior it is meant to demonstrate. The permCache value should be set to `true` to make the test meaningful.

findings.title: Per-resource cache miss now forces a full permissions DB requery on every mismatched Check call
findings.body: Previously `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` returned the cached permission map unconditionally whenever any entry existed for the user+action, regardless of whether it covered the requested resource, so a single cache entry served all Check calls for that action for the whole 30s TTL. Now, `Check` calls `getCachedIdentityPermissions` and, if the cached map doesn't contain the specific requested scope, always falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` which performs a full DB permissions query (deduplicated via singleflight only for truly concurrent calls). For workloads that call Check sequentially for many distinct resource names under the same action (e.g. authorizing each item of a list one at a time), every resource not already present in the cached scope map now triggers its own DB round trip, and is only protected from repeat DB hits via the new per-resource permDenialCache (keyed by name+parent) on subsequent identical calls. This can multiply DB load roughly proportional to the number of distinct resources checked, compared to the previous single-query-per-TTL-window behavior, and is not bounded/debounced beyond the exact (name, parent) tuple.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric mislabels a used-but-denying cache lookup as a cache miss
findings.body: When `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns a cached permission map (err == nil) but `checkPermission` evaluates it as not allowed, the code falls through to the line `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc()`, recording this as a cache miss even though the cache was actually read and used to make a (negative) decision before falling back to the DB. This mislabels cache effectiveness, making dashboards built on this metric appear to show a lower cache hit rate than what is actually happening, which could mislead capacity planning/alerting based on this metric.
